story_text.value:
I have been working with sphinx and recently wanted to have a single CLI to manage docs with support for graphs, PDF and work with RestructuredText and Markdown (CommonMark). Personally I like rst as its a specification based markup with proper extensions available.

So together with Ronak and Kanak build guidedog. It builds HTML documentation sites and PDF books from reStructuredText and Markdown. It is written in Odin. Its conversion engine is Guidedoc.

In order to develop it created few packages like implementation of Jinja and pygments in odin which can be used independently as well.

Would love to hear community feedback and hopefully it is a useful.

Documentation and details at: https://insanai.github.io/guidedog/

story_text.value:
We decided to make parts of our company database public.

This particular views shows partnerships for selected Austrian Deep Tech/Robotics startups / companies.

The data is still messy - entity resolution at scale (& cost effective!) is hard. But it already helped analyzed Go-To-Market patterns for these companies and map out trends in a client-project (i. e. "where is the robotics market going?")

Our long-term goal is to expand it into a comprehensive company database for the European market (starting with DACH) covering "soft data" such as partnerships, expansion signals (new hires, new sites, patent filings) or management changes.

story_text.value:
During this summer I wanted to start a side project, and I got the idea of embedding image search directly on your browser. This wasn't a new idea for me as i had built it at work as a small internal tool for me to search the company icons semantically instead of scrolling in the company deck.

This week (October 2026) Google released EmbeddingGemma 2, which puts text, images, audio and video in the same vector space, so I moved the app over to it from the siglip2 model i was using before. The main differences I've seen, apart from video and audio support, are the multilingual capabilities, and the better understanding of long queries, although it still struggles with generic images being too "in the middle" of the embedding space and ranking high on unrelated searches.

I know small SaaS products like this are a tough sell these days. I built it anyway because I grew up learning to code by hand, reading about solo developers with crazy ideas shipping little products that made some side money, and I wanted to go through that whole process myself: build it, deploy it, and put it in front of people.

How it works:

The model runs in your browser, transformers.js, WebGPU or WASM, depending on your device. It does work on mobile, although image upload do take way too much there.

Your files and their vectors are stored on the server so collections sync across devices. I know this could be a privacy concern, but at least for me the ease of use is worth it.

For quantisation im using fp16 on desktop with capable GPUs and q4 on any other device.

The big caveat is that first visit downloads the model (about 170 MB, or about 520 MB on desktops with fast WebGPU), it's cached after that, but you do have to wait a bit.

You can try it for free without an account on the example collections. As a side not, i took the travel photos (the Photography collection, from Venice) and the flower photos myself. There’s a free tier if you want to upload your own files, and paid plans if you need more.

If you have this problem too, I hope this shows that searching your own files using embedding models is genuinely useful, whether you use this or build your own. And if you’d rather not build it, I’d be happy to have you as a user. Any feedback is very welcome.

title.value: Show HN: Running EmbeddingGemma2 on the Browser

story_text.value:
# What is and whats not

Korosta is a privacy-first user-customizable tool to highlight job postings based on how frequent are those, and your ratings: * how often the job postings appeared to the user -> fade repeatedly seen job postings * learns from your ratings with a simple local model -> highlight relevant ones * 2 versions: free and pro * almost everything is kept local (ratings, recipes, customizations, history), only licensing and payments require a server * no account required to use it (just when doing the purchase)

This is not a job tracker, job board, or automated application system. It just annotates what you already have visible in your browser's tab.

## Links

chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/korosta/dhpnogbefak... firefox: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/korosta/

Howto create recipes fast (With the help of a LLM): https://covatools.com/korosta/howtos/create-cookbook-with-an... Website (with ultra short videos): https://korosta.app

# Why

This idea started like 2 years ago, when I was laid off from a tech company (2024's common rounds), and I started the stressful job searching. For job searching, my main platform was, and still is, linkedin: I perfected my url parameters so I can easily have my 10 different tabs. But one questions that commonly had, was "Have I already seen this job post?", and honestly, I wont be saving manually every item in a tool like trello (or the new ones). That question plus my bad memory had me with: "that role is awesome!!! ohhh I already seen it... but 2 months ago" (something like job posting recycling? maybe).

The main objective of this tool/extension is to reduce the load / fatigue of remembering what you have already seen (and not in just a single site), and also highlight what could be interesting to you personally (by learning with your ratings) -> less time searching, and thus, giving more time to apply in the relevant ones, or doing something else (like recovering your energy).

One thing I also spent time around was in the customization / editor (+ the howto in the page), so almost anybody can extend the tool (recipes/cookbook) <- I get frustrated when I love a tool but I fully depend on the developer

# beyond the technical part (more context... you can skip it, and test already)

Around 16.5 years ago I wanted to develop and sell apps, like the trend in those days... I did not. One year ago, I was thinking the same with the first version, the tool was working (even though over engineered), but I got discouraged by myself by reading all the terms of services, legal + fiscal topics, all the things that I did not know... plus some sites are very aggressive with their terms of use and tools like this.

I got a job, then changed my career path to a contractor, and meanwhile I started looking for a job again, but since the end of 2025 I really understand the new difficulties of the job market + not being sooo young, so I took the previous tool, refurbished it but with a different mindset: customization first with a simple learning algorithm so it can highlight interesting jobs to the user -> the name of the tool "Korosta" means highlight in Finnish (its difficult to find a good name ha).

I do think that is even more relevant to release it now because of AI: some platforms are pushing heavily their AI-based search engines, that are not so easy yet to customize -> putting more stress / burden on us.

In terms of monetization, I defined it based on: I am not keen of subscriptions, I grew up with shareware (like Doom... you can guess my age now), and when a single payment give you something (I wont distribute this in floppies, though). And it ended like: pay once and keep for the same major version.

I learned a lot, and I am still learning, with this development, so I want to hear your comments. Also, If you are looking for a job right now, how does the extension feel to use?

title.value: Show HN: Korosta – Remember and highlight job postings you've seen

story_text.value:
Hi everyone! I’ve been on leave since welcoming our first child into the world which has given me time, in between 3 am diaper changes and with the tireless support of Claude, to get to personal projects.

One of those is a game for my wife who’s big into word searches. Around the time she expressed interest in wanting a word search game I was reminded of “1 million chessboards” (https://eieio.games/blog/one-million-chessboards/) and thought that would be fun to replicate in this space. Thus was born infiniword - an infinite, persistent, procedurally generated, realtime multiplayer word search game.

Alongside the standard word search features, Infiniword has the following unique ones:

Scrabble like tile multipliers (currently a 1/2000 chance for a tile to be worth 3x)

First find bonuses for being the first to find a word globally

25 achievements of various difficulties

All time and weekly leaderboards across points, found words, and first finds

Simple friends list with the ability to teleport to them and hunt for words together

Shareable events like a specific word you found, winning a “wanted word”, placing in the top 3 of a “challenge zone”, and more.

“Wanted words” - a timed hunt for a specific word in a circular area that comes with a bonus based on how much time is left

“Challenge zones” - every 3 hours a random 100x100 tile zone becomes a “challenge area” where you compete with all other players to get the most points from words in the zone.

“Daily challenge zone” - same thing as the main world challenge zones but the world is just the 100x100 area with a new seed each day. Competition runs from 10am central US to 10 pm central US. The first daily launches here soon, go check it out! https://infiniword.com/daily

Hope everyone enjoys playing it as much as my family and I do!

title.value: Show HN: InfiniWord – infinite multiplayer word search

story_text.value:
Hi, I built Quaesito, a self-hosted quiz-night app for playing with friends. I thought it might be useful to others, so I wanted to share it here: https://github.com/ggirelli/quaesito

It runs on your laptop, which you can cast or screen-share on to a TV. Friends then connect and answer from their phones, as long as everyone is on the same local network. It support Windows, macOS, and Linux, although I have only tested it on Linux so far, so feedback on the other platforms would be very welcome.

I was especially careful to make it work over your local network. No requests are sent to third-party services.

I wanted something that made quiz nights more fun than just a slideshow or a PDF, with support for different types of question formats and multimedia. I have plenty of ideas for additional formats, but I wanted to keep the first release manageable.

The project was built entirely through vibe-coding, using Claude Code in an iterative process. I have released it under the MIT license and would appreciate any feedback, particularly from people who try running an actual quiz night with it.

Hope you find it useful, and have as much fun with it as I have!

Original post from my blog: https://ggirelli.info/blog/2026/10/11/quaesito

story_text.value:
It’s designed for people who are alcohol dependent and want to get visibility and control over their drinking in order to cut down or stop. Fully offline, better features than many paid apps, and free/opensource as i don’t believe in profiting from misery https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/groglog-drink-tracker/id681713...

it has stuff like burndown charts and tapering features to help people manage their reduction in medically safe ways which i felt was missing from the existing options

https://groglog.io

Some cool stuff

- daily/weekly/monthly reporting and charts so you can see how you’re doing relative to previous days/weeks

- lock screen widget so you can log a drink in two taps - super easy ux so you can log just like “beer” or a specific brand/size depending on how accurate you want to be

- HealthKit integration so you can see how drinking is affecting your resting heart rate and HRV

- three different tapering modes so you can have a budget and reduce safely

- iCloud sync for if you switch phones

- it’s pretty and extremely lightweight

It’s a bit UK centric with regards to brands but there’s no reason it couldn’t be used in other places

The main inspiration was Drink Coach as it’s delightfully simple, but lacked certain things like being able to visualise your cadence or set a dynamic budget etc

title.value: Show HN: GrogLog, a Free Drink Tracker

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

The other day I had to do some work with a lot of large animated WebP files on my Macbook running Safari and noticed that it handles them very poorly. They load slowly and it seems like they're constantly being decoded, also with really poor performance. Here's a website with similar images to what I was working with: https://colinbendell.github.io/webperf/animated-gif-decode/w...

On that website, my M1 Macbook Air decodes the boat and smoke images at fewer than 5FPS, and the brown underwater office one has a constant stutter. The performance on my iPhone 15 Pro is very similar with the additional annoyance that I have to manually "Play" each animation.

This was one of those small things that bothered me during my work week so on the weekend I decided to see if I can do something about it. I started by experimenting with the decoder itself and noticed that if you decode a static WebP image it's pretty fast - approximately as fast as other browser engines. It's actually fast enough to fit in 0.16ms. So I thought "what if I just take the WebP animation decode the frames one by one with the internal decoder and just plonk them on a canvas" and after quickly vibe coding the experiment, the images on the test page played at 60FPS flawlessly.

So I reported the issue to Apple, and then made an extension that will find animated WebP images in webpages and swap them out for the same trick. Have a look here: https://github.com/IliaMManolov/safari-animated-webp-extensi...

It's currently GitHub-only and I've spent about a day on this all-in-all but I hope anyone that has to interact with similar images in the future finds it useful. Let me know if there's interest in this too, I'd happily put it on the App Store if I can somehow have the extension cover the developer fee.

title.value: Show HN: A Safari extension to accelerate animated WebP images

Hi HN!

The other day I had to do some work with a lot of large animated WebP files on my Macbook running Safari and noticed that it handles them very poorly. They load slowly and it seems like they're constantly being decoded, also with really poor performance. Here's a website with similar images to what I was working with: https://colinbendell.github.io/webperf/animated-gif-decode/w...

On that website, my M1 Macbook Air decodes the boat and smoke images at fewer than 5FPS, and the brown underwater office one has a constant stutter. The performance on my iPhone 15 Pro is very similar with the additional annoyance that I have to manually "Play" each animation.

This was one of those small things that bothered me during my work week so on the weekend I decided to see if I can do something about it. I started by experimenting with the decoder itself and noticed that if you decode a static WebP image it's pretty fast - approximately as fast as other browser engines. It's actually fast enough to fit in 0.16ms. So I thought "what if I just take the WebP animation decode the frames one by one with the internal decoder and just plonk them on a canvas" and after quickly vibe coding the experiment, the images on the test page played at 60FPS flawlessly.

So I reported the issue to Apple, and then made an extension that will find animated WebP images in webpages and swap them out for the same trick. Have a look here: https://github.com/IliaMManolov/safari-animated-webp-extensi...

It's currently GitHub-only and I've spent about a day on this all-in-all but I hope anyone that has to interact with similar images in the future finds it useful. Let me know if there's interest in this too, I'd happily put it on the App Store if I can somehow have the extension cover the developer fee.
hits.title: Show HN: A Safari extension to accelerate animated WebP images

story_text.value:
I was driving, listening to European Hit Radio, the host hyping up the top 20, and thought, hmm, this is basically the same script every day. Could this be AI? I have some experience in voice AI, so I had the parts lying around. A few hours and several slop sessions later: Canarics Radio.

It ended up talk only news instead of music (for now, maybe AI music next?). Why - music royalties are the actual expensive part of radio. Two AI hosts discuss the day’s headlines in Latvian and English, 24/7. They know they’re AI and joke about it on air.

It’s cheap: about 1 euro a day per station in model calls. Not a lot of code either, about 400 lines of dependency free Node plus ffmpeg, but who reads code anymore, right? There is no streaming server: episodes are rendered to HLS chunks in a bucket, and the "live" playlist is a pure function of the wall clock. A stateless endpoint computes what’s playing "now", every listener hears the same thing, and if generation fails the wheel just loops. Silence is impossible.

The silly part: leave your phone number on the page and my voice agent calls you back, takes your question, and the hosts answer it in the next episode (Europe, US, CA, AU, NZ numbers).

Happy to answer questions about my music taste. Though as you already know I listen to EHR pop, the answer is: none.

title.value: Show HN: My radio station calls its listeners

story_text.value:
Hi, I'm Jakub and I used to dream to publish a novel before turning 40, but life is life -- yesterday was my 40th birthday and I'm publishing a game instead.

A few months ago I started experimenting with building a turn based tactics game with a combat system heavily inspired by the Battle for Wesnoth. The main reason was that I could not make Wesnoth work on my phone :D I iterated on it over and over, polishing graphics, finding background music, balancing units, and here it is. There is a fully playable skirmish mode -- 3 factions x 3 units x 3 levels. AI opponent, 4 difficulty levels, fog of war, time of day changing unit stats, various terrain types and traits (poison, healing, others). It runs in the browser and -- if you choose to sign in -- it syncs across devices. You can start on desktop and finish on mobile.

I wanted to make it casual, but also serious at the same time. For me many games are either too complex and require much time (like most of 4x) or too naive in terms of combat system or graphics (like many mobile games).

I'm developing campaigns -- I already have a rough scenario for the first campaign, and the first playable match (not released yet). My main focus is on single player game, while there is also a multiplayer in progress.

My goal was to make all game modes free and with no ads. There is a single paid feature -- verified play, which basically means we verify your games server side, so you can participate in future global ranks. I'm not sure if that's enough to cover costs, but we'll see.

I’m still a dev with a full-time job. Hexnoth is so far mostly a hobby project, and it's fulfilling in terms of artistic expression and storytelling. I won't create the next Baldur's Gate or Age of Wonders, but I feel great power and agency, and I can shape it nearly entirely the way I want. Or the way you'd like to have it -- just drop a message.

title.value: Show HN: Wesnoth wouldn't run on my phone -- I rebuilt the combat in the browser
